event: VXE-815 transitioned to hover about 300 ft AGL over a cliff-top LZ, showed CLIMB ABORT - LIFT SYSTEM FAULT and would not descend; the pilot slid it laterally and made a very slow manual descent to a safe landing about 15 minutes later.
component: wind-generated lift on the wing in hover (updraft at cliff-top landing site)
failure_mode: on-shore wind and vertical air currents over the cliff produced more wing lift than the light aircraft weighed, so the lift motors ran near minimum and the vehicle could not descend
contributing: light aircraft with high aspect ratio wing
moderate on-shore wind at cliff-top LZ
no manual guidance on how to descend when wing lift exceeds weight
same aircraft had the same event before (VXEP-1480)

evidence.quote: a CLIMB ABORT - LIFT SYSTEM FAULT caption was displayed and the UA did not begin its descent
this is backed up with low power-draw on the lift battery and the vertical lift motors being seen to start/stop whilst in the hover
It is holding station in VTOL with motors bouncing off the rails low
this same issue has come of a number of times. And the described assessment of the situation and the actions that were taken are in line with those other incidents.

team_view_in_comments: operators should be prepared to address a situation where too much lift is generated by the wings to descend

would_settle_it.what: lift motor throttles at minimum, HLB current and wind estimate during the hover; confirm this is the October flight and not the August VXEP-1480 data
what triggered the CLIMB ABORT - LIFT SYSTEM FAULT caption, since it is not explained by excess lift alone

reasoning: The operator saw low HLB power draw and lift motors starting and stopping in the hover, meaning the wing was carrying the aircraft. On the earlier identical event on the same tail (VXEP-1480) engineering saw the motors bouncing off their lower limit and judged it outside wind limits. Engineering said this event matches the earlier ones, and the corrective action is a manual update for wind lift.
notes: The only attachment has the same file name as the August 2025 AAR on VXEP-1480 (AAR_V815_20250819T160210Z), so the attached data may be from the earlier event rather than this October sortie. The LIFT SYSTEM FAULT caption is not explained anywhere in the ticket. No Root Cause field; team view taken from a comment. Review change: agrees_with_team was yes, scored against the engineers' view in comments; set to no_team_answer because the ticket has no Root Cause field.

event: VXE 593 (fuel cell D4500799) aborted a VTOL launch on a magnetometer failure and landed safely; after landing and disassembly the fuel cell was found smoking and smoldering inside the nose.
failure_mode: fuel cell smoldering after shutdown and disconnection; cause not found
contributing: possibly incomplete fuel cell cool down before removal (customer not sure)
launch abort from VTOL magnetometer disturbance, attributed in VXEP-1554 to rebar in the concrete pad
same fuel cell later RMAd from VXE 820 after failing to charge the HLB in flight

evidence.quote: Okay, I am just asking as the video they sent shows the fuel cell actively smoldering while being unplugged from the vehicle.
Normal cooldown would bring internal temperatures below 150°C, and the adhesives on the fuel cell will not melt or smolder at that temperature (RTV is tolerant to 315°C).
I believe we let the fuel cell go through its normal cool down after the aborted landing but I cant be sure.
there is a pretty significant disturbance in the mag readings right when the vtol system spools up.
there was most likely rebar or some type of metal in the concrete pad that was flown from when the abort occurred.

team_view_in_comments: I informed them that it was likely adhesives burning in

would_settle_it.what: where the smoke comes from on the fuel cell and whether it is still powered or hot
location of heat damage or burnt material on the fuel cell

would_settle_it.file: RMA-973 teardown of fuel cell D4500799
would_settle_it.what: heat damage, burnt wiring or adhesive inside the stack and electronics
fuel cell temperature and shutdown or cool down sequence after the aborted launch

attachments_read: 58508_CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form - 820_930_929_fuel cell.pdf.md
reasoning: The ticket shows the fuel cell smoldering while being unplugged, and the customer could not confirm a normal cool down. The fuel cell engineer ruled out adhesives at normal cool down temperatures, and the field test or RMA findings were never recorded. The ticket was closed because the same unit was later RMAd from VXE 820 for not charging the HLB, but the RMA tickets hold only blank forms, so the smoke cause is not determined.
notes: Clone of VXEP-1554, which covers the magnetometer abort (closed as probable rebar in the concrete pad). Fuel cell D4500799 later flew on VXE 820 (VXEP-1794, RMA-973); VXEP-1794 closed as SOFC operating as designed. RMA-973 and RMA-970 attachments are blank forms or image-only scans. No Root Cause field. Review change: agrees_with_team was differs, scored against the engineers' view in comments; set to no_team_answer because the ticket has no Root Cause field. The disagreement with that comment view was: The field engineer told the customer it was "likely adhesives burning in", but the fuel cell engineer rejected that: "the adhesives on the fuel cell will not melt or smolder at that temperature (RTV is tolerant to 315°C)". No inspection or test result in the ticket or its links explains the smoke, so the cause stays not determined.

event: VXE-881 (Block 35X with LEMB) got a VTOL GPS fault in the primary landing pattern, rerouted to the ELZ and would not do a vertical Land Immediately after repeated commands; after the gimbal was turned off and a Silvus node added it landed normally in the PLZ.
failure_mode: VTOL GPS fault between IP4 and IP5 sent the vehicle to the ELZ by design; Land Immediately with ELZ selected gives a glide landing, so the vertical landing never happened
contributing: Land Immediately behavior with ELZ selected not described in the manual
OGCS did not show the ELZ radio button as selected after the automatic reroute
possible L1 jamming in the area
same aircraft and LEMB showed CAN bus damage a week later (VXEP-1608), and VTOL AP GPS data comes over CAN

evidence.quote: When the VTOL gets a GPS Fault during the Primary Landing Pattern (between IP4 and IP5, in particular), the vehicle will go to the ELZ after passing IP5 and before attempting to transition.
If the LAND NOW button is pressed, the vehicle will perform a glide land immediately.
There are questions as to whether L1 jamming was present at the time of the flight as 3MBDE also experienced an inflight E140 GPS fail during their operations
document that LI while the ELZ is selected will result in glide landing on the current flight path.
likely CAN due to fixed wing ap data is off serial while vtol ap data is off CAN for GPS

would_settle_it.what: VTOL AP GPS quality, satellite count and CAN error counts at the time of the VTOL GPS fault
the full incident analysis, including any finding on why the VTOL GPS faulted
parent investigation of Land Immediately not accepted

reasoning: FS2-3923 reproduced the behavior in test: a VTOL GPS fault in the landing pattern reroutes to the ELZ and Land Immediately then gives a glide landing, so the landing logic worked as designed. The real degraded input was the VTOL GPS fault, whose cause is not found; candidates are L1 jamming or early CAN damage on this aircraft, which a week later lost VTOL GPS data over CAN.
notes: Scored as a designed abort on a degraded VTOL GPS input. The link to the later CAN failure on 881 (VXEP-1608) is my inference from timing and the shared LEMB, not stated by engineers. The FS2-3923 report pptx is not in the export.

contributing: ground setup changed between flights (SGCS2 wired, then SGCS1 with mag mounts)

evidence.quote: After the aircraft launched, transitioned, and flew through WP1, the aircraft immediately lost comms.
they ran a spectrum scan and there was significant noise on the frequency they were using so they switched frequencies
second flight SGCS1 with MAG Mounts. aircraft was good on the ground.

team_view_in_comments: there was significant noise on the frequency they were using so they switched frequencies

would_settle_it.what: Silvus GUI link and noise readings at the time of the dropout
radio RSSI and link quality over the flight, and whether later flights on the new frequency were clean

event: VXE-886 did not launch after the launch wizard: the User Landing Control window opened and closed within seconds and the launch was cancelled; GCS logs show the operator pressed the abort button on the joystick.
component: GCS joystick (Xbox controller) launch abort button
failure_mode: student operator pressed abort on the controller before liftoff, so the GCS briefly showed then closed landing controls with the vehicle safe on the ground
contributing: Xbox controller plugged in during launch

evidence.quote: The GCS logs indicate the operator aborted the launch using the abort button on the joystick.
There was an XBOX controller plugged in.
I talked with the instructor last night and they were fairly certain that the student clicked abort on the controller.
it seems like the system behaved as expected and briefly presented the landing controls before closing them due to the vehicle being safe on the ground.

team_view_in_comments: The GCS logs indicate the operator aborted the launch using the abort button on the joystick.
reasoning: The GCS logs show an abort command from the joystick before launch was detected, and the instructor confirmed the student pressed abort. The GCS then behaved as designed, opening and closing the landing controls because the vehicle was still on the ground. The RC mode change seen in the data is explained by the plugged-in Xbox controller, with RC not enabled in GCS.ini.
notes: No Root Cause field. Could also be read as no fault found for the aircraft, since the system responded correctly to the operator input. Review change: agrees_with_team was yes, scored against the engineers' view in comments; set to no_team_answer because the ticket has no Root Cause field.

event: VXE-674 in U-Drive gave a Low energy/low endurance warning and auto RTB'd and landed while showing 57% main battery and 26.6 V; the investigation could not explain the trigger.
component: low energy RTB logic (XCOMM endurance and recovery calculation)
failure_mode: low energy RTB triggered when the logged range, speed and SOC give about 97 recoveries against a 1.2 threshold; suspected corrupted value in the calculation after a roll fault, not proven
contributing: roll fault from prolonged U-Drive turn commands about 2 minutes before the RTB
turret and fuel cell link fault flags set at the same time
slow data logging rate (1 sample per 20 s) hides short transients

evidence.quote: Time: 042:19.000  Vehicle low energy RTB: 0.000000  0.000000
Approximately 97 recoveries possible at that distance and SOC. The threshold needed to trip the RTB is 1.2 recoveries. A low energy RTB does not make sense in this situation.
Leading theory is that an unlikely corruption event occurred and triggered an incorrect warning.
I see that the event occurred in the GCS debug log, but there is no indication of a low power RTB in the XCOMM event log or the datalog.

team_view_in_comments: Leading theory is that an unlikely corruption event occurred and triggered an incorrect warning.

would_settle_it.what: high rate values of wind vector, ground speed, range and SOC at the RTB time to find an input that would drive the recovery count below 1.2

would_settle_it.file: HIL test of low energy RTB after roll fault
would_settle_it.what: whether a roll fault during U-Drive can corrupt the wind or speed inputs to the RTB calculation

reasoning: The XCOMM event log in the FS2-4161 report does record a vehicle low energy RTB, so the aircraft logic made the decision. Putting the logged range, ground speed and SOC into the RTB equation gives about 97 possible recoveries, far above the 1.2 trip level, so the logic acted on a bad input or a fault inside the calculation. No direct evidence of which, so this stays narrowed to the low energy RTB software.
notes: The FS2-4161 report is titled AC 467 and its file is named V647, but its contents refer to T95_V674 and match this event. It conflicts with the ticket comment that the XCOMM event log showed no low power RTB. Report gives 66% SOC at the RTB versus 57% reported by the operator. Closed as cannot reproduce; team view taken from the linked report.

event: VXE 881 (Block 35X with LEMB 3-L0042) could not get a GNSS fix in OGCS and SUAV reported CW not detected, although the .10 page and satellites were visible; swaps showed the fault in the fuselage and the aircraft was repaired by replacing every board on the CAN bus.
component: LEMB battery controller (BMS) CAN interface, LEMB 3-L0042
failure_mode: LEMB CAN node added a ground loop and transients above component ratings on the aircraft CAN bus, damaging the CAN transceivers on XCOMM, GNSS interface board, VTOL AP and ADP (able to receive but not transmit)
contributing: Block 35X CAN bus over-terminated (XCOMM, VTOL AP and ADB terminations)
damaged or failed TVS diodes on the LEMB battery controller
CAN transceiver chips not tolerant to faults, ESD and temperature

evidence.quote: We attached three separate CWs to 881s fuselage and were unable to connect to them in SUAV but could access the .10 page for each one.
Replacing GNSS Interface V3 inside avionics box resolved issue. Will acquire the removed part for further inspection.
Vehicle was repaired after replacing all boards on the CAN bus network. All CAN chips were damaged from LEMB stress to the CAN bus network.
We weren't able to recreate the failure, but we were able to demonstrate that the 35X configuration causes transients that exceed the component ratings on the diodes that failed.
It has been determined that the TVS diodes on the battery controller are either malfunctioning, installed backwards, or damaged.
likely CAN due to fixed wing ap data is off serial while vtol ap data is off CAN for GPS

team_root_cause: Introduction of LEMB induced electrical stress to the vehicle’s CAN bus which severely degraded or disabled all CAN transceiver chips.

would_settle_it.file: decapsulation or cross section of removed CAN transceivers
would_settle_it.what: confirm the transmit side FETs failed as suspected on the XCOMM and GNSS interface board chips

would_settle_it.file: B35x CAN LEMB battery investigation II.pptx
would_settle_it.what: transient measurements on the 35X CAN bus with and without the LEMB data cable
CAN error counts and missing VTOL GPS messages

reasoning: Center wing swaps both ways put the fault in the 881 fuselage, the VTOL AP lost GPS data that arrives over CAN, and replacing the GNSS interface board and the other CAN boards restored function. VXEP-1880 found the LEMB CAN node pulls the bus differential low, its controller TVS diodes are faulty, and the 35X setup produces transients above the diode ratings, which went away with the LEMB data cable unplugged. The failure was not recreated and the chips were not decapped, so confidence is medium.
notes: LEMB 3-L0042 itself was not in the batch of LEMBs measured in VXEP-1880 (3L-0028, 0030, 0032 were), so the LEMB mechanism is by similarity. RMA-854 intake PDF is image-only. Same LEMB and aircraft as VXEP-1592 a week earlier.

event: VXE-894 and VXE-897 (USSS) did not auto RTB after their final racetrack on two days; the operator commanded RTB after about four minutes, and after restarting SUAV the next flight auto RTB'd with about a two minute delay.
component: mission end auto RTB (exit from final racetrack after mission timer expiry)
failure_mode: vehicle kept flying the last racetrack past the mission timer and RTB'd late or not at all
contributing: SUAV left open from the previous flight (restart appeared to help)
GCS 6.5.1 with BLK30 Adv Nav type 115

evidence.quote: The aircraft did not RTB after the expiration of the last primary mission element. It did RTB eventually to the PLZ, and before Auto Low Battery RTB would have done it.
The aircraft kept flying the racetrack through the timer expiration, and eventually RTB’d to IP1 at around the 16:57 elapsed time mark.
After fully closing and reopening SUAV, we launched the aircraft again with no issues.
Expected behavior (based on investigation): Vehicle continues last racetrack and does not RTB. Actual behavior: vehicle continues successfully RTBs after finishing the last racetrack

team_view_in_comments: Issue unclear. unable to reproduce. Customer has not reported issue again. Probabale cause; Software Issue.

would_settle_it.what: mission timer, nav mode and waypoint state when the last racetrack ended, and any RTB command
same for the second aircraft
how the final racetrack and its timer are defined in the mission

reasoning: Both aircraft and one HIL run kept circling the last racetrack after the mission element timer expired and only RTB'd minutes later, while a second HIL run RTB'd normally. That points to the mission end RTB logic, with a possible link to the SUAV session state, but nothing names a module. Engineering closed it as a probable software issue that could not be reproduced.
notes: Two aircraft on one ticket (894 and 897); 894 is the tail field. Not clear whether the fault lies in the autopilot or in SUAV mission handling; I picked vehicle_software because the aircraft decides when to leave the racetrack, but ground_software is a credible alternative. Closed and added to the Bermuda Triangle list. No Root Cause field; team view from the Executive Summary. Review change: agrees_with_team was yes, scored against the engineers' view in comments; set to no_team_answer because the ticket has no Root Cause field.

event: VXE 491 with customer CW 4036 transitioned to VTOL and began descending, then at about 230 ft AGL the VTOL system stopped and the aircraft crashed; closed as a duplicate of VXEP-1314.
component: Main System Harness connector to avionics enclosure (black Alden)
failure_mode: connector not fully mated after an avionics enclosure swap, came unmated from vibration and cut power to the avionics during VTOL descent
contributing: aircraft used as a test bed for spare avionics enclosures, so the harness was un-mated and re-mated
no reassembly quality check on test assets

evidence.quote: at approx 230ft AGL I lost SA Camera Feed and ground crew (Artis B.) reported the VTOL system had failed, causing AC to crash into the ground.
when taking the avionics box out of the fuselage, the grey debug connector was the only one connected.
This is a look at where each processor stops logging by correlating VTOL Throttles. All logging stops within 5.22 seconds.
host vtol state was, is: APVTOL_TAXILZ APVTOL_DESCENT
Beyond verifying the circumstances, there is no further way to prove this, but it aligns with info.

reasoning: VXEP-1314 found all processors stopped logging within about 5 seconds just after the VTOL descent began, with no power anomaly before that, which fits a loss of avionics power. On teardown the black Main System Harness connector was found unplugged from the avionics box, which had recently been swapped. Engineering notes this cannot be proven further, so confidence is medium.
notes: Canceled as a duplicate of VXEP-1314; analysis taken from that ticket and the team view quoted is the VXEP-1314 Root Cause field. VXEP-1314 event logs (about 160 KB each) were read with repeated TRACE, ISR, GCS query and version lines filtered out. GPS fault was due to velocity uncertainty
